tally.headline: 3 of 10 gradeable claims held up, 4 did not

implied_side.why: EdgeDesk’s own number sat 1.7 points toward Green Bay Packers of the quote EdgeDesk captured at nflverse reference. That is what the disagreement implied. It was published as research, not as a recommendation to bet it.

implied_total.why: EdgeDesk’s fair total of 40.9 sat 5.6 points below the captured total of 46.5.

closing_line.note: The line moved 0.5 points toward the side EdgeDesk’s number leaned before kickoff. That is the market arriving where EdgeDesk already was, and over many games it is the only evidence that a disagreement carried information.

reasons: 4 of 8 gradeable claims went the other way. The read of this matchup was wrong in its mechanism, not only in its number.
EdgeDesk projected a home margin of 0.8 and the game finished 17 the home way — 16.2 points of margin error, inside the range the model published.
process.basis: the drivers, matchups and measured advantages only — never the price or the market claim, which are the result in longer words

verdict.line: The number did not land and the reasoning did not either. This is the case that should change something, and the lessons below say what.

grading.separation_note: The bet result and the process grade above are computed separately and are allowed to disagree. A winning number with a broken thesis is recorded as exactly that.

lessons.pregame_expectation: Points scored and allowed, opponent-adjusted — Green Bay Packers by 0.8 points — worth -0.8 of the EdgeDesk number, in Green Bay Packers’s favour.
lessons.actual_result: Green Bay Packers 22 points against Minnesota Vikings 39.
lessons.lesson: EdgeDesk named Green Bay Packers as better in scoring and the game went the other way. One game does not overturn a season-long rating, but this is the direction to watch: every signal this claim rests on went the other way

lessons.pregame_expectation: 2 of the claims in this article rested on model.
lessons.actual_result: None of them could be graded: no single-game statistic in EdgeDesk’s vocabulary observes this driver.
lessons.lesson: EdgeDesk prices these games partly on signals it has no way to observe afterwards. That is not an error in the model — it is a gap in the audit, and it means the platform cannot tell, from results alone, whether those parts of the number are earning their weight.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Consider whether a postgame data source exists for model.

lessons.pregame_expectation: EdgeDesk published a fair total of 40.9.
lessons.actual_result: The game finished with 61 points, an error of 20.1.
lessons.lesson: A total missed by this much usually means a pace or a finishing assumption was wrong, not that both ratings were. Check which of the two moved.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Was the play count or the points per drive the miss? Both are in this game’s result record.

lessons.pregame_expectation: EdgeDesk makes it Minnesota Vikings -0.8 where the market has Minnesota Vikings -2.5 at nflverse reference — a 1.7 points disagreement.
lessons.actual_result: Minnesota Vikings won by 17. the result landed on EdgeDesk’s side of the market number: Minnesota Vikings beat a margin of 2.5
lessons.lesson: The disagreement landed. One landing proves nothing on its own; the aggregate of them, held against the closing line, is the only thing that would.
